entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute
entries.description:
Run multiple commands in ONE call. Every command's output is auto-indexed into the knowledge base; if you also pass `queries`, the matching sections come back in the same round trip so a follow-up search call is not needed.

Concurrency parallelizes the FETCH phase (run-the-commands). The DERIVATION phase — turning raw output into an answer — still belongs in code: add a processing command that consumes the indexed output and prints only the answer, so the raw bytes never enter your conversation (Think-in-Code, same principle as the sandbox tool).

WHEN:
  - You have 3+ related commands you would otherwise run sequentially (multi-issue lookups, git log + git diff + git blame, multi-file reads, multi-region cloud queries)
  - You want to gather AND query in one round trip — pass `queries` so the matching sections come back inline
  - You want to parallelize I/O-bound work — pass `concurrency` 2-8 (network calls, gh CLI, cloud APIs, multi-repo git reads)
  - The combined output is large enough that piping it through ctx_search later would itself be expensive — let auto-index + inline queries do both in one shot

WHEN NOT:
  - Single command with no follow-up query — run it in the sandbox tool directly
  - CPU-bound or stateful commands — keep concurrency at 1 (npm test, build, lint, port-binding servers, lock-file holders, anything that races on the same resource)

RETURNS:
  Auto-indexed section list per command label, plus top matches per query (when `queries` is passed). Raw output is NOT echoed in full — only the matched windows. Concurrency>1 switches each command to its own per-command timeout (no shared budget); concurrency=1 preserves the legacy shared-budget cascading-skip-on-timeout path. Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches; keep at 1 for CPU work or shared-state commands; lower the value when target hosts enforce per-IP rate limits.

EXAMPLE: ctx_batch_execute(
  commands: [
    {label: "issue 1", command: "gh issue view 1"},
    {label: "issue 2", command: "gh issue view 2"},
    {label: "summarize", command: "echo done"}
  ],
  queries: ["root cause", "proposed fix"],
  concurrency: 2
)

label.description: Section header for this command's output (e.g., 'README', 'Package.json', 'Source Tree')

commands.description: Commands to execute as a batch. Output is labeled with the section header. Default order is sequential; pass concurrency>1 to run in parallel (output stays in input order).

queries.description: Search queries to extract information from indexed output. Use 5-8 comprehensive queries. Each returns top 5 matching sections with full content. This is your ONLY chance — put ALL your questions here. No follow-up calls needed.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs. With concurrency=1, the value (when set) is a shared budget across commands; with concurrency>1, it is applied per-command.

concurrency.description: Max commands to run in parallel (1-8, default: 1). Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches (network, gh, curl, multi-repo git reads). Keep at 1 for CPU-bound (npm test, build, lint) or stateful commands (ports, locks). >1 switches to per-command timeouts (no shared budget) and individual `(timed out)` blocks instead of cascading skip.

cwd.description: Optional working directory for all shell commands in this batch.

query_scope.description: Scope for `queries` (default: `batch`). `batch` searches ONLY the chunks produced by this batch's commands — useful when you want answers about the just-fetched output. `global` searches the entire persistent index (same scope as ctx_search) — useful when you want the batch commands to enrich context and the queries to also surface related prior knowledge in one round trip.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute

code.description: Source code to execute. Use console.log (JS/TS), print (Python/Ruby/Perl/R), echo (Shell), echo (PHP), fmt.Println (Go), IO.puts (Elixir), or Console.WriteLine (C#) to output a summary to context.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs (which is the right layer for this policy). Pass an explicit value for long-running builds (Gradle/Maven/SBT).

background.description: Keep process running after timeout (for servers/daemons). Returns partial output without killing the process. IMPORTANT: Do NOT add setTimeout/self-close timers in background scripts — the process must stay alive until the timeout detaches it. For server+fetch patterns, prefer putting both server and fetch in ONE ctx_execute call instead of using background.

cwd.description: Optional working directory for shell commands. Non-shell languages still execute from their sandbox temp directory.

intent.description:
What you're looking for in the output. When provided and output is large (>5KB), indexes output into knowledge base and returns section titles + previews — not full content. Use ctx_search(queries: [...]) to retrieve specific sections. Example: 'failing tests', 'HTTP 500 errors'.

TIP: Use specific technical terms, not just concepts. Check 'Searchable terms' in the response for available vocabulary.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file
entries.description:
Read a file into a sandboxed FILE_CONTENT variable and run code over it. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation — the file bytes stay in the sandbox.

Think-in-Code applied to file-level analysis: Reading the whole file means every byte enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. Running code over it here lets you keep the raw bytes out and only the derived answer in. Same principle as ctx_execute, scoped to one named file via the FILE_CONTENT variable.

WHEN:
  - You want to KNOW SOMETHING ABOUT a file (line count, matches of a pattern, parsed structure, statistical aggregate) without needing to SEE all of it
  - The file is structured (CSV, JSON, log, code) and a code-level derivation is cheaper than reading verbatim
  - The file is large enough that reading the full content would burn meaningful conversation memory you need for the actual work
  - The derivation may itself produce a large output you want recall-by-topic on later — pass an `intent` string; outputs over ~5KB are auto-indexed and only matching sections come back, retrievable via ctx_search

WHEN NOT:
  - You intend to EDIT the file — use Read so the subsequent Edit can match the exact text
  - You only need one specific line and you know its offset — Read with offset/limit is the simplest path
  - The file is small AND you will consume all of it for understanding/editing — Read directly

RETURNS:
  Only what your code prints. The FILE_CONTENT variable holds the raw bytes inside the sandbox; nothing else leaves. When `intent` is set and output exceeds the auto-index threshold, the response carries searchable section titles + previews instead of the raw stdout.

EXAMPLE: ctx_execute_file(path: "huge.log", language: "javascript", code: "const errs = FILE_CONTENT.split('\\n').filter(l => /ERROR|FATAL/.test(l)); console.log(`${errs.length} error lines`); console.log(errs.slice(-5).join('\\n'))")
EXAMPLE: ctx_execute_file(path: "data.csv", language: "javascript", code: "const rows = FILE_CONTENT.split('\\n'); console.log(`rows: ${rows.length - 1}, header: ${rows[0]}`)")

path.description: Absolute file path or relative to project root

code.description: Code to process FILE_CONTENT (file_content in Elixir). Print summary via console.log/print/echo/IO.puts/Console.WriteLine.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs.

intent.description: What you're looking for in the output. When provided and output is large (>5KB), returns only matching sections via BM25 search instead of truncated output.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index
entries.description:
Fetches URL content, converts HTML to markdown (JSON is chunked by key paths, plain text indexed directly), persists it in a searchable knowledge base, and returns a small preview window per source. The raw page bytes never enter your conversation — they live in storage and you retrieve any section on-demand via ctx_search.

Caching: every fetch is cached on disk and reused for repeat calls within the TTL window. The default TTL is 24 hours; override per-call with the `ttl` parameter (milliseconds, `ttl: 0` bypasses cache like `force: true`). Stored content older than 14 days is cleaned up on startup.

WHEN:
  - You need web content (docs, changelogs, API references, spec pages) and the raw page bytes should NOT enter your conversation
  - Multi-URL research (library evaluation, migration scans, doc comparisons): pass the `requests` array and a `concurrency` value 2-8 for parallel I/O
  - You want repeat lookups against the same URL to be cheap (TTL cache hits return only a hint, no re-fetch)
  - You want a long-lived cache window (override `ttl` upward for stable specs) or a guaranteed-fresh fetch (`ttl: 0` or `force: true`)

WHEN NOT:
  - You already have the content locally — store it via the inline index tool
  - The page is SPA-rendered (JavaScript-required to materialize content) — this is a plain HTTP fetch, no headless browser

RETURNS:
  Per-source preview windows extracted around indexable headings plus indexing metadata (chunk counts, source labels, cache state). Raw content is NOT echoed back — retrieve any section on-demand via ctx_search(source: "<label>"). Concurrency parallelizes the fetch phase up to your chosen value (capped by the host's logical CPU count); the FTS5 write phase always runs serially because SQLite is a single-writer store. Net latency = max(fetch latency across the pool) + sum(per-source index write time). Cache hits skip both phases and return a small freshness hint instead of re-fetching. Use 4-8 for stable I/O-bound batches; lower the value when the target host enforces a per-IP rate limit you cannot raise.

EXAMPLE: ctx_fetch_and_index(
  requests: [{url: "https://react.dev/...", source: "react"}, {url: "https://vuejs.org/...", source: "vue"}],
  concurrency: 5
)

url.description: Single URL to fetch and index (legacy single-shape)

source.description: Label for the indexed content when using single `url` (e.g., 'React useEffect docs', 'Supabase Auth API'). For batch, put source in each requests entry.
Label for this URL's indexed content

requests.description: Batch shape: array of {url, source?} entries. Use with concurrency>1 for parallel fetch. Each request indexed under its own source label. Output preserves input order.

concurrency.description: Max URLs to fetch in parallel (1-8, default: 1). Use 4-8 for I/O-bound multi-URL batches (library docs, changelogs, pricing pages). Capped by os.cpus().length on small machines (response notes when capped). Indexing is always serial regardless — only fetches race.

force.description: Skip cache and re-fetch even if content was recently indexed

ttl.description: Override the cache freshness window for this call, in milliseconds. `ttl: 0` bypasses the cache like `force: true`; omit to use the default 24h TTL.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
entries.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). File-backed sources carry a content hash and auto-flag staleness when the source file changes.

WHEN:
  - You want to recall something that exists in storage (recently indexed content, prior session events, auto-memory) instead of re-reading raw sources
  - You have multiple related questions about the same body of knowledge — batch every question into one call (the ranking pipeline runs per-query but the round-trip cost is paid once)
  - You want to scope the query to one labelled source (pass `source` — partial match is fine)
  - You want a chronological view across current session + prior sessions + persistent auto-memory (pass `sort: "timeline"` — the default `relevance` mode only ranks within the current session)
  - You want to filter ranked results by content shape (pass `contentType: "code"` to surface implementation snippets or `contentType: "prose"` to surface explanations)

WHEN NOT:
  - The data you want to query has never been stored in the knowledge base AND no session memory has accumulated around it — capture first (run a gather-and-index call), then come back here to query
  - You have one ad-hoc question against data that is not in the knowledge base — answer it inline by running code in the sandbox tool; one round-trip instead of capture-then-query

RETURNS:
  Per-query ranked sections with window-extracted snippets. Use 2-4 specific technical terms per query. Common session-memory source labels: `decision` (user corrections / preferences), `error` and `error-resolution` (past failures + their fixes), `blocker`, `plan`, `user-prompt`, `rejected-approach`, `compaction` (post-compact session guide). See ctx_stats for live category counts. Each response carries a throttle counter (call #N/M in the rolling time window); results taper toward the soft cap and calls block after the hard cap. Tune via CONTEXT_MODE_SEARCH_WINDOW_MS, CONTEXT_MODE_SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS_AFTER, CONTEXT_MODE_SEARCH_BLOCK_AFTER.

EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["root cause", "proposed fix", "test coverage"], source: "issue-#683")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["what did we decide about caching"], source: "decision", sort: "timeline")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["useEffect cleanup pattern"], source: "react-docs", contentType: "code", limit: 5)
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["last user prompt", "active skills", "open blockers"], sort: "timeline")

queries.description: Array of search queries. Batch ALL questions in one call.

source.description: Filter to a specific indexed source (partial match).

contentType.description: Filter results by content type: 'code' or 'prose'.

sort.description: Sort mode. 'relevance' (default): BM25 ranked, current session only. 'timeline': chronological across current session, prior sessions, and auto-memory.

project.description: Project scope. Default (omit): this session's project — auto-resolved from the host adapter. 'global': span every project in the shared store (cross-project recall). <absolute-path>: scope to that specific project directory.

  "doi": "10.1186/s40798-026-01006-z",
  "abstract": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 observational studies (3,209 athletes) comparing revision and primary ACL reconstruction on return to sport, return at preinjury competition level, time to return and psychological readiness, with searches up to November 2024.",
  "tldr": "Athletes after revision ACL reconstruction returned to sport less often, returned at their preinjury level less often, took about 1.2 months longer, and reported lower psychological readiness than after primary reconstruction. The differences come from observational studies, so plan for a longer, more psychologically demanding return rather than expecting a similar outcome.",
  "methods": "Systematic search of Web of Science, EMBASE and PubMed up to 15 November 2024 for observational studies comparing revision and primary ACL reconstruction on return-to-sport outcomes or psychological readiness. Methodological quality was assessed with MINORS and certainty of evidence with GRADE; meta-analysis of odds ratios and standardized mean differences; registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024600347).",
  "findings": "Revision patients had lower odds of return to sport (OR 0.66, 95% CI 0.49-0.89; 73% vs 79%) and lower odds of return at the preinjury competition level (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.36-0.76). Time to return was 1.2 months longer (SMD 0.38; p = 0.004), and psychological readiness was lower (SMD -0.75, 95% CI -1.14 to -0.36; about 14.2 points). Heterogeneity for overall return to sport was low (I2 = 16%).",
  "limitations": "Only observational studies were included, follow-up was mostly short to medium term, and data on sex, sport type and level of play were limited.   "practicalImplications": "Staff managing an athlete after revision ACL reconstruction should expect a lower return-to-sport rate, a lower chance of returning at the preinjury competition level, a slightly longer timeline, and lower psychological readiness than after primary reconstruction.  "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Performance", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Soccer", "Rugby", "Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Female Athletes", "Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) searching six databases on 1 May 2025, with 582 titles and abstracts screened, 74 full texts assessed and seven studies included. Across these studies, uncertainty, fear, lack of confidence and poor social support were perceived barriers to return to sport and physical activity, while confidence, motivation, strong social support and athletic identity were perceived facilitators.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The evidence base is seven studies drawn from soccer, rugby union, Gaelic and Australian football, at mixed levels of play, and the synthesis is narrative with no effect estimates. It cannot show that psychosocial factors cause differences in return to sport.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat these barriers and facilitators as measured predictors of return to sport, when they are perceived experiences reported by a few studies and the review does not show that changing them improves outcomes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Meredith S, Farley JB, Hunt J, Dent E. The Role of Psychosocial Factors in Returning to Physical Activity and Sport Among Female Football Players After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Scoping Review. Sports Med Open. 2026;12:148.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s40798-026-01118-6",
  "abstract": "Scoping review of seven studies on psychosocial factors and return to physical activity and sport in female football players after anterior cruciate ligament injury. Fear, uncertainty, low confidence and poor social support were barriers, while confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity were facilitators.",
  "tldr": "For female footballers after an ACL injury, fear, uncertainty, low confidence and weak social support were reported as barriers to return. Confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity were reported as helpers, so build these into the return plan alongside the physical milestones.",
  "methods": "Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR with a prospective protocol. Six databases (SCOPUS, CINAHL, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, PsycInfo and Embase) were searched on 1 May 2025, and two reviewers screened records against eligibility criteria: original research on psychosocial factors and return to sport or physical activity in female players of any football code with an ACL injury, managed surgically or non-surgically, and mean participant age of 18 or older. Findings were synthesized narratively into themes.",
  "findings": "Seven studies were included. Across them, uncertainty, fear, lack of confidence and poor social support were perceived barriers to return at a lower competition level and to physical activity. Confidence, motivation, strong social support and athletic identity were perceived facilitators, helping players return at their preinjury level or at a lower level.",
  "limitations": "Only seven studies were included, and the findings are narrative themes from perceived experiences rather than effect estimates. The authors call for more high-quality research focused specifically on female footballers, with greater consideration of sex and gender in study design.",
  "practicalImplications": "Return-to-sport planning for female footballers after ACL injury should include fear, confidence and social support alongside physical milestones. The authors discuss psychologically informed, exposure-based approaches to fear of reinjury, but the review does not test any screening tool or intervention.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff working with female footballers should track confidence, fear and social support alongside physical testing, because these were reported to shape how players return to their level. The evidence is perceptual and does not set performance targets.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to return-to-sport planning in female footballers after ACL injury: fear, uncertainty, low confidence and poor social support were reported as barriers, and confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity as facilitators. It cannot set return criteria, and it does not show whether addressing these factors changes return rates."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q12",
 "sourceFile": "Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction - a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Rehabilitation", "Sports Medicine", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Network meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials (n = 797) of resistance training after primary ACL reconstruction in adults or adolescents, comparing blood flow restriction, isokinetic, eccentric and other modalities with standard multimodal rehabilitation. Blood flow restriction ranked first for quadriceps strength (SMD 0.40 vs standard rehabilitation, 95% CI 0.07-0.73) and quadriceps mass (SMD 0.82, 95% CI 0.11-1.53), and eccentric training ranked first for quality of life (SMD 1.31 vs standard rehabilitation, 95% CI 0.01-2.63); isokinetic training ranked highest for knee function, but differences among active modalities were not significant.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Several contrasts rest on few trials (PT and IKT in particular), protocols, cuff pressures, loading and follow-up varied widely, and the comparator was usual rehabilitation rather than a single standard. The sample was not restricted to athletes, so the trial populations are not described as athletes in the source.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the isokinetic SUCRA ranking for knee function as proof that isokinetic training is the best option, when the authors state that pairwise differences among active modalities were not significant and there is no clear evidence of superiority.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Chen J, Wu Y, Xu H, Ren Y, Yang R, Yao S, et al. Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Front Physiol. 2026;17:1792091.",
  "doi": "10.3389/fphys.2026.1792091",
  "abstract": "Network meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials (n = 797) comparing resistance training modalities after primary ACL reconstruction on quadriceps strength, quadriceps mass, knee function and health-related quality of life, using SUCRA rankings.",
  "tldr": "Blood flow restriction training ranked best for quadriceps strength and mass compared with usual rehabilitation, and eccentric training for quality of life. Isokinetic training ranked highest for knee function, but no active modality clearly beat the others on that outcome, so choose the modality to match the target.",
  "methods": "Searches of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science and Google Scholar to 30 September 2025 for randomized trials in adults or adolescents after primary ACL reconstruction that compared resistance-based modalities with standard multimodal rehabilitation or with each other. Outcomes were pooled as standardized mean differences, modalities were ranked by SUCRA, and network consistency was assessed with a design-by-treatment interaction model.",
  "findings": "Twenty-two trials (n = 797) were included. Blood flow restriction training ranked first for quadriceps strength (SUCRA 81.7; SMD 0.40, 95% CI 0.07-0.73 vs standard rehabilitation) and quadriceps mass (SUCRA 79.1; SMD 0.82, 95% CI 0.11-1.53 vs standard rehabilitation). Isokinetic training had the highest ranking for knee function (SUCRA 87.7), but pairwise differences among active modalities were not statistically significant. Eccentric training ranked first for quality of life (SUCRA 87.4; SMD 1.31, 95% CI 0.01-2.63 vs standard rehabilitation).",
  "limitations": "The network was uneven, with few trials for some contrasts (PT and IKT in particular), which limits precision for head-to-head comparisons. Heterogeneity in intervention parameters, outcome instruments and follow-up windows could not be modeled with study-level data, and residual confounding is possible. Time since surgery, graft type and kinetic chain configuration were inconsistently reported.",
  "practicalImplications": "Match the resistance modality to the outcome: blood flow restriction training for quadriceps strength and mass, and eccentric training for quality of life, both compared with usual rehabilitation. Do not treat isokinetic training as clearly superior for knee function, since the pairwise differences among active modalities were not significant.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance and rehabilitation staff can use the ranking to choose a resistance emphasis that fits a quadriceps or quality-of-life goal after ACL reconstruction. The review does not test sport-specific performance outcomes such as sprinting, jumping or change of direction.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to rehabilitation after primary ACL reconstruction, where blood flow restriction ranked first for quadriceps strength and mass. The review does not measure time to return to sport, sport readiness or re-injury, so it cannot be used to decide when an athlete can return."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q15",
 "sourceFile": "Acute-chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports - a multilevel meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Acute:chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports: a multilevel meta-analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "Rugby"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and three-level multilevel meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies and trials in team-sport athletes. Of 41 eligible studies, 16 (797 athletes) were pooled, and elevated acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) showed a small-to-moderate association with injury risk (Hedges g 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.54; I2 = 95.8%), stronger for contact and non-contact injuries and not significant for time-loss injuries.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Heterogeneity was very high (I2 = 95.8%), several moderator analyses rested on few studies, and ACWR calculation methods, time windows, load metrics and injury definitions varied. The review shows association only and cannot establish causation or prediction.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the pooled g of 0.35 as a 35% increase in injury risk, which the authors explicitly reject, and treat ACWR as a stand-alone injury predictor, which they also reject.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Ding L, Weldon A, Xu J, Malone S, Sampaio J, Zhang Z, et al. Acute:chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports: a multilevel meta-analysis. Front Public Health. 2026;14:1896651.",
  "doi": "10.3389/fpubh.2026.1896651",
  "abstract": "Systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of the association between acute:chronic workload ratio and injury risk in team-sport athletes. Of 41 eligible studies, 16 (797 athletes) were pooled, showing a small-to-moderate association with injury (g = 0.35).",
  "tldr": "In team-sport athletes, a high acute:chronic workload ratio was associated with a small-to-moderate increase in injury risk, most clearly for contact and non-contact injuries. The authors conclude it is a contextual monitoring indicator to use within a multi-marker load-management approach, not a stand-alone predictor.",
  "methods": "Four electronic databases searched from inception to October 2024. Prospective cohort studies or trials in team-sport athletes reporting ACWR and injury outcomes were included; effect sizes were converted to Hedges g and pooled with a three-level random-effects model, with moderator analyses by injury type and other study characteristics. Registered in PROSPERO (CRD420245127618).",
  "findings": "Of 41 eligible studies, 16 studies involving 797 athletes were included in the meta-analysis. Elevated ACWR was associated with higher injury risk (g = 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.54; I2 = 95.8%). Associations were stronger for contact and non-contact injuries, and not significant for time-loss injuries or other moderators.",
  "limitations": "Residual statistical dependence may remain when several outcomes, time windows or workload metrics come from the same cohort. Several moderator analyses rested on few studies, reducing power to detect subgroup differences. Load metrics, time windows and injury definitions varied across the included studies, and heterogeneity was very high.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use ACWR as a contextual monitoring indicator within an individualized, multi-marker load-management system, not as a stand-alone causal or predictive model. The authors state that the pooled effect should not be read as a 35% increase in injury risk.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff can track ACWR alongside other load and wellness markers to watch workload trends, but should not use it as a stand-alone injury predictor. The review addresses injury risk, not performance outcomes.",
  "rtp": "Limited relevance to return to sport: the review covers injury risk in team-sport athletes, not rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loading or clearance."
 }
}

  "abstract": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 studies (404 participants) comparing resisted and unresisted sprint training on linear sprint, vertical jump and change-of-direction performance in athletes.",
  "tldr": "Resisted sprint training improved linear sprint and change-of-direction performance, and its advantage over unresisted sprinting was clearest for the 0-10 m sprint. The change-of-direction advantage was borderline, and the jump and COD estimates rest on few studies.",
  "methods": "PRISMA review of seven databases (PubMed, Web of Science, MEDLINE, CENTRAL, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Embase) from inception to 12 July 2025. Studies compared resisted sprint training with unresisted sprint training or regular training in competitive or recreational athletes; GRADE was used for certainty; analysis in Stata/MP 18.0.",
  "findings": "Within-group, RST improved linear sprint (SMD 0.65), COD (SMD 1.10) and vertical jump (abstract prints SMD -0.38, p = 0.013). UST improved linear sprint (SMD 0.42) and COD (SMD 0.60) but not vertical jump (SMD -0.03). RST beat UST for COD (p = 0.043), with larger benefits for 0-10 m sprint (p < 0.001) and in youth athletes; RST beat regular training for linear sprint and vertical jump but not COD (p = 0.064).",
  "limitations": "Sport type, sex, training level, sled load, sprint distance and training volume varied across studies, and most studies involved male soccer players, limiting generalisation to female athletes and other sports.   "practicalImplications": "When the goal is initial acceleration and change of direction, prioritise resisted sprint training. For broader explosive power, the authors suggest pairing it with vertically oriented strength or plyometric training.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff can use resisted sprinting as a sprint and change-of-direction option, most clearly for acceleration over 0-10 m. If jump power is also a target, pair it with vertical strength or plyometric work.",
  "rtp": "Not designed for return to sport: the studies were in trained athletes and the review does not assess injury outcomes, so it cannot guide reintroduction of sprint loading after injury. The authors name injury prevention and risk as a research need."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q19",
 "sourceFile": "The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of 10 controlled trials in competitive male and female soccer players (aged 15 to 45), comparing cold-water immersion (CWI) with control or placebo after match or simulated match play. CWI improved recovery of maximal voluntary contraction (SMD 1.02, 95% CI 0.55-1.50) and countermovement jump (SMD 0.38, 95% CI 0.12-0.64, evident at 48 h only), reduced creatine kinase (SMD -0.77, 95% CI -1.17 to -0.37) and reduced soreness (SMD -1.04, 95% CI -1.91 to -0.17), with no effect on 20 m sprint (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -1.41 to 0.23).",
 "screeningLimitations": "The included studies were small and blinding of participants and researchers was not possible with CWI, so bias is likely. Every outcome's 95% prediction interval includes a null effect, so the authors advise cautious reading.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat CWI as a proven recovery aid for sprint performance or for every post-match outcome, when sprint showed no effect and all prediction intervals include null.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Veen J, Bergh C, Cao Y, Randers MB, Krustrup P, Edholm P. The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2026;36:e70202.",
  "doi": "10.1111/sms.70202",
  "abstract": "Systematic review with meta-analysis of 10 controlled trials of cold-water immersion after match or simulated match play in competitive soccer players, measuring sprint, countermovement jump, maximal voluntary contraction, creatine kinase and soreness at 24 to 72 hours.",
  "tldr": "After soccer match play, cold-water immersion improved recovery of maximal strength, reduced creatine kinase and reduced soreness, with a small jump gain at 48 hours. It did not improve sprint recovery, and the prediction intervals are wide enough to include no effect.",
  "methods": "Systematic database search for peer-reviewed controlled trials comparing CWI with control or placebo after match or simulated match play in competitive soccer players, with outcomes at 24, 48 or 72 hours: 20 m sprint, countermovement jump, maximal voluntary contraction, creatine kinase and delayed-onset muscle soreness. Random-effects meta-analysis of standardised mean differences with 95% CIs and prediction intervals; PEDro scale for quality; publication bias assessed qualitatively.",
  "findings": "CWI improved MVC recovery (SMD 1.02) at all time points and CK recovery (SMD -0.77) at all time points. CWI improved CMJ (SMD 0.38), but only at 48 hours. Soreness was reduced at 24 and 72 hours (SMD -1.04). 20 m sprint was unaffected (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -1.41 to 0.23). The prediction intervals for all outcomes included a null effect.",
  "limitations": "Blinding of participants and researchers is impossible with CWI, so bias is possible. The included studies had small samples, which limits statistical power. Publication bias was assessed only qualitatively, and the prediction intervals include null effects.",
  "practicalImplications": "CWI after match play may help soccer players recover strength and reduce soreness and muscle damage markers, but not sprint performance. Because the jump benefit appears only at 48 hours and the prediction intervals are wide, expect modest and variable effects.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff can consider CWI as one post-match recovery tool for strength and soreness, not as a sprint-recovery tool. Timing matters, since the jump benefit appeared only at 48 hours.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to recovery after match play in players who are not injured. The review does not study injured players or return-to-play decisions, so it cannot inform clearance or rehabilitation loading."
 }
}

 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Soccer", "Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and fragility-index meta-analysis of nine randomized controlled trials (474 patients) comparing platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection with rehabilitation or placebo for acute muscle injuries. PRP shortened time to return to sport (mean difference 7.5 days overall, p < 0.001, fragility index 188), with a larger effect in double-blind trials (MD 8.8) and hamstring trials (MD 7.5). No difference was found in re-injury or complication rates.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only nine trials with 474 patients, four rated low risk of bias by RoB 2, and GRADE rated the outcomes as limited quality. Few trials reported pain (VAS), and the fragility indices for re-injury and complications were small (5 and 7).",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat PRP as a proven way to shorten return to sport after any muscle injury, when the main result has a fragility index of 188 patients, the evidence is limited quality, and the pain benefit appeared only in hamstring trials.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Bensa A, Fattini Fellini G, Boffa A, Grassi A, Samuelsson K, Filardo G. Platelet-Rich Plasma Accelerates the Return to Sport in Athletes with Acute Muscle Injuries: A Systematic Review and Statistical Fragility Index-Based Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Sports Med Open. 2026;12:55.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s40798-026-01017-w",
  "abstract": "Systematic review and fragility-index meta-analysis of nine randomized trials (474 patients) comparing platelet-rich plasma injections with rehabilitation or placebo for acute muscle injuries. PRP shortened time to return to sport, with no difference in re-injury or complications.",
  "tldr": "Platelet-rich plasma injections shortened return to sport after acute muscle injury by about 7.5 days versus control in these trials. The evidence is of limited quality and the pain benefit appeared only in hamstring trials, so treat PRP as a possible adjunct rather than a standard fix.",
  "methods": "PRISMA systematic search of PubMed, Cochrane Library and Web of Science in January 2026 for English-language RCTs comparing PRP injection with rehabilitation or placebo for acute muscle injury. Outcomes were time to return to sport, VAS pain, re-injury and complications, with sub-analyses of double-blind trials and hamstring trials. Fragility index and continuous fragility index were calculated; risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE.",
  "findings": "PRP gave faster return to sport overall (MD 7.5 days, p < 0.001; CFI 188), in double-blind trials (MD 8.8, p < 0.001; CFI 67) and in hamstring trials (MD 7.5, p = 0.001; CFI 97). PRP gave greater pain relief only in the hamstring sub-analysis (VAS MD 0.4, p = 0.006; CFI 22). Re-injury and complication rates did not differ (FI 5 and FI 7).",
  "limitations": "Few studies and patients limited precision, and only a few trials reported VAS. Fragility indices were small for re-injury and complications. RoB 2 ratings were mixed (four low risk, five high risk), and GRADE rated the evidence as limited quality.",
  "practicalImplications": "PRP can be considered as an option to shorten return to sport after acute muscle injury, mainly as shown for hamstring injuries. Because the evidence is of limited quality, it should not be relied on as the main driver of rehabilitation.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance and medical staff should plan return-to-sport timelines with PRP as a possible shortening factor, not a guaranteed one. The review measures return timing and pain, not performance after return.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to return to sport after acute muscle injury, mainly hamstring injury. It shows faster return in pooled trials but cannot establish performance after return or effects in non-hamstring injuries."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q22",
 "sourceFile": "Return-to-sport rate and time in elite athletes after ankle syndesmosis injuries - a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Return-to-sport rate and time in elite athletes after ankle syndesmosis injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["American Football", "Ice Hockey", "Rugby"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies (901 elite athletes) with ankle syndesmosis injuries, using random-effects logit-transformed pooling. The pooled return-to-sport rate was 96% (95% CI 93-98%; I2 = 27%), with 98% after suture-button fixation and 98% after nonoperative management. Time to return averaged about 58 days across studies, summarised descriptively.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Time-to-return data were inconsistently reported and often lacked variability measures, so no formal pooling was possible. Funnel-plot asymmetry and Egger's test (p = 0.0002) suggested publication bias.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could expect a 96% return rate and a 58-day timeline for any elite athlete, when the timeline is a descriptive average from inconsistently reported studies and publication bias was suggested.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Li R, Sun C, Qi P, Xu Z. Return-to-sport rate and time in elite athletes after ankle syndesmosis injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Orthop Surg Res. 2026;21:69.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s13018-025-06566-6",
  "abstract": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies (901 elite athletes) with ankle syndesmosis injuries, pooling return-to-sport rate and summarising time to return. Pooled return to sport was 96%, with similar rates after suture-button fixation and nonoperative management.",
  "tldr": "Most elite athletes returned to sport after ankle syndesmosis injury (pooled 96%), typically within about two months. Treatment type did not change the pooled return rate, but time to return was inconsistently reported and only summarised descriptively.",
  "methods": "Systematic search of five databases through September 2025 for return-to-sport outcomes in elite athletes with syndesmotic ankle injury. Pooled return proportions used random-effects models with logit transformation; time outcomes were synthesised with random-effects models or descriptively. Subgroup, sensitivity and meta-regression analyses were run; quality was assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; publication bias with funnel plots and Egger's test.",
  "findings": "Fourteen studies (901 elite athletes) were included. The pooled return-to-sport rate was 96% (95% CI 93-98%; I2 = 27%). Suture-button fixation gave 98% and nonoperative management 98%. Average time to return was about 58 days. Funnel-plot asymmetry and Egger's test (p = 0.0002) suggested publication bias.",
  "limitations": "Time-to-return reporting was inconsistent and often lacked measures of variability, which precluded a formal meta-analysis; the 58-day average therefore has limited inferential value. Publication bias was suggested.",
  "practicalImplications": "Most elite athletes can expect to return to sport after a syndesmosis injury whatever the treatment, with most resuming play within about two months. The authors say management should still be individualised by injury severity and sport demands.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff can use the pooled return rate and the roughly two-month timeline as planning benchmarks for elite athletes, with the caveat that timing data are descriptive and publication bias was suggested.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to return-to-sport planning for elite athletes with syndesmotic ankle injury: pooled return of 96% and a descriptive timeline of about two months. It cannot set individual return criteria, because time data were not pooled."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q23",
 "sourceFile": "Comparative efficacy of portable active cooling vs. passive cooling for reducing core temperature in exertional heat stroke - a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Comparative efficacy of portable active cooling vs. passive cooling for reducing core temperature in exertional heat stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Healthy Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (PRISMA 2020; PROSPERO CRD420261292698) of 11 randomized and crossover trials (148 participants) comparing portable active cooling with passive cooling in adults with exercise-induced hyperthermia. Active cooling lowered core temperature faster (MD 0.02 deg C/min, 95% CI 0.01-0.03, p < 0.00001); the gain came from external refrigerant-based devices (type A, MD 0.04 deg C/min), while wearable pre-cooling devices (type B) showed no advantage.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 11 trials with 148 participants, with poor allocation concealment and outcome-assessment blinding, and most participants were healthy volunteers, athletes or military personnel with exercise-induced hyperthermia rather than classical heat stroke patients. The outcome is cooling rate, not clinical outcome.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the overall cooling gain (0.02 deg C/min) as enough to treat exertional heat stroke faster or to improve survival, when the trials were small and the review measured cooling rate, not clinical outcomes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Shi C, Zhang T, Xia L, Shi W, Qu J, Song L, et al. Comparative efficacy of portable active cooling vs. passive cooling for reducing core temperature in exertional heat stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Public Health. 2026;14:1811173.",
  "doi": "10.3389/fpubh.2026.1811173",
  "abstract": "Systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA 2020) of 11 randomized and crossover trials (148 participants) comparing portable active cooling with passive cooling for reducing core temperature in adults with exercise-induced hyperthermia.",
  "tldr": "External refrigerant-based portable cooling lowered core temperature faster than passive cooling, and the advantage was clearest above 30 deg C ambient. Wearable pre-cooling devices showed no clear advantage, so choose devices by cooling mechanism rather than portability.",
  "methods": "PRISMA 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420261292698) of randomized and crossover trials comparing portable active cooling (type A: external refrigerant-based; type B: wearable pre-cooling) with passive cooling in adults with exercise-induced hyperthermia. The primary outcome was mean core temperature cooling rate (deg C/min), pooled with a random-effects model; subgroup analysis by device type and ambient temperature; risk of bias rated across domains.",
  "findings": "Eleven trials (148 participants) were included. Active cooling cooled faster than passive cooling (MD 0.02 deg C/min, 95% CI 0.01-0.03, p < 0.00001). Type A devices were superior (MD 0.04 deg C/min, 95% CI 0.02-0.04), particularly when ambient temperature exceeded 30 deg C. Type B devices showed no significant advantage (MD 0.00 deg C/min).",
  "limitations": "The evidence base is small (11 trials, 148 participants). Allocation concealment and blinding of outcome assessment were poor, and several trials had unclear risk in other domains. The authors note that limitations are inherent to exertional heat stroke research, which makes direct clinical trials hard to run.",
  "practicalImplications": "For field management of exertional heat stroke or severe exercise-induced hyperthermia, prefer external refrigerant-based portable cooling over passive cooling. Choose devices by cooling mechanism rather than portability, since wearable pre-cooling showed no clear advantage.",
  "athleteDev": "Medical and performance staff managing hot-weather training can use the finding that refrigerant-based active cooling cooled faster than passive cooling, especially above 30 deg C. The evidence measures cooling rate, so it does not show that a device changes clinical outcomes.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to heat-illness management during training and competition, not return to play. The review measures cooling rate in hyperthermic adults and does not test return-to-activity decisions after heat stroke."
 }
}

 "screeningLimitations": "The recommendations are consensus based and draw on limited direct trials, and the authors note limited return-to-play evidence for eating pathology and for adolescents. Energy availability is hard to measure outside laboratory settings, which the authors acknowledge.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the cumulative risk assessment as a validated tool that settles clearance or return-to-play decisions, when the guidance is consensus based and the tool's link to bone health rests on a single study of 239 collegiate athletes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Williams NI, De Souza MJ, Misra M, Nattiv A, Joy E, Barrack M, et al. 2025 Update to the Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement Part 2: Clinical Guidelines for Screening, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Return to Play for Adolescents and Adults. Sports Med. 2026;56:375-427.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s40279-025-02332-0",
  "abstract": "Second part of the 2025 Female Athlete Triad consensus update, with revised clinical guidelines for screening, diagnosis, treatment, and clearance and return to play for adolescent and adult athletes, including eating disorders, bone loss, menstrual disturbance and a cumulative risk assessment.",
  "tldr": "The revised Triad guidance covers screening, treatment, and clearance and return to play for adolescent and adult female athletes. It moves away from an energy-availability threshold and adds a cumulative risk assessment, but the return-to-play recommendations are consensus based and need individual clinical judgment.",
  "methods": "Consensus process by an expert writing group, following the 2014 Female Athlete Triad consensus approach: one in-person group meeting, several virtual video meetings and e-mail communication. Topics were divided among section leaders, who drafted each section with their teams.",
  "findings": "Revised recommendations cover eating disorders and disordered eating, and non-pharmacological and pharmacological treatment of bone loss and abnormal menstrual cycles. Energy-deficiency menstrual disturbance can be reversed with a moderate increase in food intake and modest weight gain, but restored menses alone do not indicate ovulation until several consecutive normal cycles occur. The Triad cumulative risk assessment scores six items from 0 to 2 and maps the total to low, moderate or high risk, which corresponds to a clearance or return-to-play decision.",
  "limitations": "The authors note limited guidance for return to play in eating pathology and that assessing energy availability has limits in real-life settings compared with laboratory conditions. The statement favours individualised, staged return-to-play decisions over fixed rules.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use the cumulative risk assessment to inform clearance and return-to-play decisions for athletes with Triad concerns. For eating pathology, the example given is that return to play should begin with low-pressure activity and move to competition only once weight status is achieved and maintained.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff should not use a fixed energy-availability threshold to judge female athletes. The guidance moves toward assessing energy deficiency with additional indicators, including menstrual, bone and metabolic markers.",
  "rtp": "Directly relevant to clearance and return to play for female athletes with Triad issues, including adolescents. Use the cumulative risk assessment and staged progression to inform decisions, but the guidance does not replace clinical judgment, and the evidence for return to play in eating pathology is limited."
 }
}

Reading depth, which is short of what you asked: I did not read every full text chunk by chunk. The eight bodies come to about 680,000 characters without references, roughly 170k tokens, which does not fit in one context. For each paper I read the header, DOI, abstract, population and methods, results, limitations and conclusions, extracted with code. Q24 (about 215,000 characters of body) was read only through its abstract, the consensus-process paragraph, the cumulative risk assessment, and the return-to-play passages. If you need a verbatim read, Q24 and Q18 are the two that need it, in a separate pass.

Judgment calls for Eric:
- Q20 EXCLUDE under (c). The pooled trials span any age, sex and health status, with no athlete subgroup reported. Creatine kidney safety is relevant to athlete supplement use, so this could reasonably be an INCLUDE. Confidence is medium.

- Q23: the trials are healthy volunteers, athletes and military personnel with exercise-induced hyperthermia, not classical heat stroke patients. I kept INCLUDE with medium confidence, and the Mixed tag covers the mix.
- Q24: a consensus statement with no sample, so the evidenceSummary describes the process. Year 2026 comes from the "Sports Medicine (2026) 56:375-427" line.
- Q18: the primary domain is Training & Performance, not Monitoring & Technology, because the paper is about the link between asymmetry and performance. Monitoring & Technology is in domains.
